photos.description: AudioMoth autonomous recording unit mounted on Acacia raddiana tree trunk at Qsar Ghilen oasis. Green waterproof housing protects microphone and data logger. Device programmed for continuous 17-hour recording cycle (April 10-11, 2026, 15:27-08:20) capturing pre-dawn, diurnal, and nocturnal acoustic activity. Acacia's fine bipinnate foliage visible, distinguishing it from date palm canopy.

Upward view of AudioMoth recorder mounted in Acacia canopy, Qsar Ghilen oasis. Clear blue sky visible through characteristic feathery Acacia foliage. Recording position selected to minimize wind interference while maximizing coverage of oasis interior and transitional edge habitats.

Zakher Bouragaoui installing AudioMoth autonomous recording unit on Acacia tree, Qsar Ghilen oasis. Field deployment methodology requires precise positioning to balance acoustic coverage with equipment security. Multi-day deployment necessitated overnight presence for equipment maintenance and concurrent nocturnal biodiversity sampling.

Transition zone between active erg (sand dune system) and oasis edge vegetation, Qsar Ghilen. Windswept sand patterns visible on right contrasting sharply with Acacia trees on left. This ecological boundary represents the interface between hyperarid desert and irrigated agricultural oasis — demonstrating abrupt habitat transitions characteristic of Saharan oases.

Spring-fed water source at Qsar Ghilen oasis showing turquoise-green pool surrounded by date palms (Phoenix dactylifera) and traditional earthen architecture. This permanent water source sustains the three-layer oasis structure and provides critical habitat for resident and migratory bird species. Water availability is the ecological driver enabling biodiversity in hyperarid landscapes receiving <100mm annual precipitation.

Am Ali (local oasis resident and knowledge holder, in traditional green clothing and white turban) with Zakher Bouragaoui at outdoor restaurant, Qsar Ghilen. Community engagement essential for contextualizing acoustic biodiversity data within traditional ecological knowledge frameworks. Local expertise provided critical context for interpreting species detections and seasonal habitat use patterns.

Pale sparrow species perched on Roman/Byzantine-era stonework at archaeological site near Qsar Ghilen. The bird's light plumage suggests Desert Sparrow (Passer simplex), a sedentary Saharan specialist distinct from the House Sparrow (Passer domesticus) detected in acoustic surveys (157 detections). Ancient ruins provide perching sites and potential nesting cavities for desert-adapted bird species.

Interior of Oasis Camp restaurant at Qsar Ghilen showing traditional woven palm-frond furniture and earthen architecture. Local infrastructure built using vernacular materials and passive cooling design appropriate for extreme desert climate. Community-based tourism provides economic diversification beyond traditional date cultivation.

Roadside landscape at Bel Khir / Ardh El Talah showing scattered Acacia raddiana trees in arid pre-desert environment. This location is recognized as one of the last remaining sites in Tunisia supporting viable populations of A. raddiana, the iconic umbrella thorn acacia of sub-Saharan savannas. Species critically threatened by overgrazing, woodcutting for fuel, and climate-driven aridity increase. Relict populations persist only in protected or culturally significant locations.

Wildlife monitoring signage at Qsar Ghilen archaeological site showing illustrated Caracal (Caracal caracal). Sign indicates planned future camera-trap or acoustic monitoring expansion to document medium-sized carnivores. Caracal populations in southern Tunisia are poorly documented; combined acoustic-visual monitoring could provide baseline data for this elusive desert predator.

Weevil (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) attracted to UV light trap on white sampling sheet, Qsar Ghilen sand dunes. Nocturnal light-trapping reveals cryptic arthropod diversity in arid ecosystems often assumed to have low species richness. Coleoptera are dominant taxa in desert arthropod assemblages; weevils fill herbivore and seed-predator niches.

Interior of traditional Berber troglodyte dwelling, Old Matmata. Underground excavation into soft sedimentary rock creates naturally climate-controlled living space — interior temperature remains stable year-round despite extreme surface conditions (summer highs >45°C, winter lows <5°C). Whitewashed walls, carved storage niches, and woven textiles demonstrate centuries-old architectural adaptation to hyperarid environment.

Hand providing scale reference for small desert ephemeral plant with white flowers, Qsar Ghilen dunes. Desert ephemerals germinate following rainfall events and complete their life cycle rapidly (weeks to months) before soil moisture dissipates. Flowering attracts specialist pollinators including desert-adapted bees and hawk moths documented via light-trap sampling. Ephemeral flora represents critical trophic base for seasonal food webs.

Hawk moths (Family Sphingidae) and smaller moth species on UV light-trap sheet, Qsar Ghilen dunes. Sphingids are strong-flying nocturnal pollinators with specialized hovering flight and long proboscis adapted to tubular desert flowers. UV light trapping complements acoustic bird monitoring to assess multi-taxa biodiversity. Moths serve as prey for insectivorous bird species including nightjars and flycatchers.

Entrance to Galaxy Tours hotel/museum at Old Matmata, primary Star Wars filming location. Troglodyte architecture famously served as Lars homestead exterior in Star Wars Episode IV (1977). Tourism infrastructure demonstrates economic diversification in marginal arid lands; film-location tourism provides alternative livelihood to agriculture and pastoralism.

Sleeping quarters in traditional Berber troglodyte dwelling, Old Matmata. Carved niches serve as built-in storage; woven textiles provide bedding. Subterranean architecture maintains thermal stability without mechanical climate control — passive cooling via thermal mass and minimal surface exposure to solar radiation.

Courtyard of traditional troglodyte dwelling, Old Matmata, showing central open-air pit surrounded by excavated living chambers. Courtyard design provides light and ventilation to underground rooms while maintaining thermal insulation. Arched doorways, earthen walls, and multi-level excavation demonstrate sophisticated vernacular architecture predating modern building technology.

Field camp tent at Qsar Ghilen oasis with date palm canopy and traditional architecture visible in background. Multi-day acoustic monitoring deployment required overnight presence for equipment security, battery replacement, and concurrent nocturnal biodiversity sampling (UV light traps for insects). Tent camp positioned within oasis interior to facilitate equipment access.

Field consultation between Zakher Bouragaoui and Am Ali at outdoor restaurant, Qsar Ghilen. Am Ali (local resident in traditional green clothing) providing ecological knowledge about seasonal bird presence, water source permanence, and historical land use patterns. Integration of local ecological knowledge with quantitative acoustic data strengthens interpretation of biodiversity patterns and informs community-based conservation approaches.

Beetle specimen (Coleoptera) on UV light-trap sheet, Qsar Ghilen dunes. Dark coloration likely serves thermoregulatory function in diurnal desert species or represents cryptic nocturnal coloration. Beetles documented during nocturnal sampling preserved for subsequent taxonomic identification by specialists.

UV light trap deployed at night on Qsar Ghilen sand dunes showing white sampling sheet illuminated by UV lamp. Methodology attracts nocturnal flying insects including moths (Lepidoptera), beetles (Coleoptera), and true bugs (Hemiptera). Light-trapping conducted concurrently with acoustic bird monitoring to assess multi-taxa biodiversity. Nocturnal insect sampling complements daytime visual surveys and provides baseline invertebrate data for arid ecosystem assessment.

Praying mantis (Order Mantodea) on sandy substrate, Qsar Ghilen. Mantids are ambush predators feeding on flying insects including flies, moths, and small beetles. Cryptic coloration provides camouflage against predators and prey. Presence indicates healthy insect prey base supporting secondary consumers in desert food web.

Dark passerine bird foraging on rocky substrate with sparse vegetation at Qsar Ghilen archaeological site. Plumage pattern suggests wheatear species (genus Oenanthe), ground-foraging insectivores characteristic of arid open habitats. Ancient ruins provide elevated perching sites for territorial display and predator vigilance.

Roman or Byzantine-era Latin inscription carved into limestone at Qsar Ghilen archaeological site. Text partially legible showing characteristic Latin epigraphy. Archaeological evidence indicates continuous human habitation of Qsar Ghilen region for millennia — oasis water sources have sustained settlements since classical antiquity. Historical land use may influence contemporary biodiversity patterns through habitat modification and species introductions.
